title: Diagrams for Time, Place and Population

blocks.html: Descriptive epidemiology asks when, where and in whom. Each question has its own diagrams: the line diagram and the epidemic curve for time (§4.5.1–4.5.2), the spot map and the choropleth map for place (§4.5.3), and the pictogram and population pyramid for population (§4.5.4–4.5.5). §4.5.6 then collects the ways graphs mislead. The data in this section are synthetic teaching data, invented for the examples.
Line Diagram and Semi-Logarithmic Graph

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A line diagram plots a quantity against time (or another ordered variable), with successive points joined by straight lines. On an arithmetic-scale graph equal distances on the y-axis stand for equal amounts. On a semi-logarithmic (semi-log) graph the y-axis is logarithmic, so equal distances stand for equal ratios, while the x-axis stays arithmetic.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
The line diagram is the standard way to show a trend: monthly malaria cases, annual infant deaths, coverage by year. The joined line invites the eye to follow the change from one period to the next. Use it when the x-axis is ordered, usually time; do not join points for unordered categories.

On a semi-log graph the distance from 10 to 100 equals the distance from 100 to 1,000 (CDC, 2012b). That makes the slope show the rate of change (the percentage change per period) rather than the absolute change. The CDC’s teaching text puts it this way: “Two or more lines following parallel paths show identical rates of change” (CDC, 2012b).

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Suppose a count grows by the same factor (1 + r) each year: yₜ = y₀ × (1 + r)ᵗ.

Take logarithms: log yₜ = log y₀ + t × log(1 + r).

This is a straight line in t with slope log(1 + r). So on a semi-log graph:

  • a constant percentage change gives a straight line;
  • two series changing by the same percentage give parallel lines, however different their sizes;
  • the steeper line is the faster-growing series in relative terms.

On an arithmetic scale, the same series curves upwards, and the larger series tends to look as if it is rising faster, because its absolute changes are larger.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Figure 4.9 shows monthly malaria cases in one district over three years (synthetic data). Each year peaks in August (256, 198 and 159 cases), after the monsoon, and the annual totals fall from 1,738 in 2023 to 1,319 in 2024 and 1,043 in 2025. The line diagram shows both the seasonal cycle and the decline.

blocks.alt: Line diagram of monthly malaria cases
blocks.caption: Figure 4.9. Line diagram: monthly malaria cases in one district, January 2023 to December 2025 (synthetic teaching data). August peaks are labelled.

blocks.html: Figure 4.10 shows annual dengue cases in a city and in a small town, 2016–2025 (synthetic data).

blocks.alt: Arithmetic and semi-log line graphs of dengue cases
blocks.caption: Figure 4.10. The same two series on an arithmetic scale (left) and a semi-logarithmic scale (right). Synthetic teaching data.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Absolute change, 2016 to 2025. City: 500 to 2,580, a rise of 2,080 cases. Town: 20 to 413, a rise of 393 cases. On the arithmetic panel the city’s line climbs steeply and the town’s line hugs the axis.
  2. Relative change. City: 2,580 ÷ 500 = 5.16-fold. Town: 413 ÷ 20 = 20.65-fold.
  3. Annual growth factor (the ninth root, since there are 9 yearly steps). City: 5.16^(1/9) = 1.20, that is 20% a year. Town: 20.65^(1/9) = 1.40, 40% a year.
  4. Semi-log slopes (log₁₀ per year). City: log₁₀ 1.2 = 0.079. Town: log₁₀ 1.4 = 0.146. The town’s line is almost twice as steep.
  5. Doubling time: solve (1 + r)ᵗ = 2 for t, giving t = log 2 ÷ log(1 + r). City: 0.301 ÷ 0.079 = 3.8 years. Town: 0.301 ÷ 0.146 = 2.1 years.
  6. Result: the city adds more cases each year, but the town’s epidemic is growing twice as fast in relative terms. Only the semi-log graph shows this at a glance.

points.html: Use an arithmetic scale to show absolute numbers (how many beds, how many cases to treat). Use a semi-log scale to compare rates of change, or to show data spanning several orders of magnitude (Bland, 2015, ch. 5, treats line graphs and logarithmic scales together).
A logarithmic axis has no zero. Label it clearly as a log scale, because many readers assume an arithmetic axis.
Seasonal data need several complete years before you judge a trend. Comparing August with December tells you about the season, not the trend.

blocks.html: Epidemic Curve

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: An epidemic curve (epi curve) is a histogram of the number of cases in an outbreak by time of onset of illness (CDC, 2012b).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Time is continuous, so the bars adjoin, as in any histogram (recall §4.3.1). The x-axis interval matters. The CDC’s convention is an interval of about one-quarter of the incubation period, and anywhere between one-eighth and one-third of it (CDC, 2012b). Too wide an interval merges the peaks; too narrow scatters single cases.

The shape suggests how the outbreak spread (CDC, n.d.-a):

  • Point source (everyone exposed at one time, such as a shared meal): “The number of cases rises rapidly to a peak and falls gradually. The majority of cases occur within one incubation period.”
  • Continuous common source (exposure goes on, such as a contaminated well): the curve “rises gradually and might plateau”.
  • Propagated (person-to-person spread): “progressively taller peaks, each being one incubation period apart”.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Figure 4.11 (left) shows 64 cases of gastroenteritis after a wedding feast; onsets run from 16:00 on day 1 to 14:00 on day 3. For this exercise, the suspected agent’s incubation period is taken as 12 to 72 hours, averaging 36 hours. An 8-hour interval is 8/36 ≈ 0.22 of the average incubation period, inside the one-eighth to one-third range. The right panel shows 38 cases of a person-to-person infection in a village: clusters of 1, 3, 8 and 17 cases about 12 days apart, then 9 cases after control measures began.

blocks.alt: Epidemic curves for a point-source and a propagated outbreak
blocks.caption: Figure 4.11. Epidemic curves. Left: point-source outbreak, 8-hour intervals (D0 = feast day). Right: propagated outbreak, 3-day intervals (synthetic teaching data).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Estimate when the wedding guests were exposed, using the CDC’s three rules (CDC, n.d.-b).

  1. Latest possible exposure = earliest onset minus the minimum incubation period, because even the quickest case needed at least 12 hours: day 1 16:00 − 12 h = day 1 04:00.
  2. Earliest possible exposure = last onset minus the maximum incubation period, because even the slowest case took at most 72 hours: day 3 14:00 − 72 h = day 0 14:00.
  3. So exposure most likely fell between day 0 14:00 and day 1 04:00.
  4. Cross-check from the peak: the tallest bar runs from day 2 04:00 to 12:00, with its midpoint at 08:00. Count back the average incubation period: day 2 08:00 − 36 h = day 0 20:00.
  5. Result: the window from day 0 14:00 to day 1 04:00 contains the feast at 20:00 on day 0, and the peak estimate points straight at it. Your next step is to compare food-specific attack rates among the guests.

points.html: An epi curve is a histogram of onsets, so the bars adjoin; mark the interval width on the axis label.
The back-calculation is only as good as the incubation period you assume for the agent. With the wrong agent in mind, the window will be wrong.
A single late case far to the right may be a secondary (person-to-person) case, or a case with an unrelated exposure; it widens the window from rule 2.
The shapes are typical, not guaranteed. Small outbreaks give ragged curves, and a point-source outbreak can seed secondary spread, giving a mixed pattern.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 4.4

questions.prompt: A district’s measles cases rose from 50 to 200 in five years, while a neighbouring district’s rose from 500 to 1,000. On a semi-log graph, which line is steeper? Give each district’s annual growth factor.
questions.answer: First district: 200 ÷ 50 = 4-fold in 5 years; annual factor = 4^(1/5) = 1.32 (32% a year). Second district: 1,000 ÷ 500 = 2-fold; annual factor = 2^(1/5) = 1.15 (15% a year). On a semi-log graph the slope is log(annual factor), so the first district’s line is steeper (log₁₀ 1.32 = 0.120 vs log₁₀ 1.15 = 0.060 per year), even though the second district added more cases (500 vs 150).

questions.prompt: In a point-source outbreak the first case fell ill 30 hours after a community lunch and the last 90 hours after it. The agent’s incubation period is taken as 24 to 96 hours. Using the first- and last-case rules, where does the exposure window fall relative to the lunch?
questions.answer: Latest possible exposure = first onset − minimum incubation = 30 − 24 = 6 hours after the lunch. Earliest possible exposure = last onset − maximum incubation = 90 − 96 = −6, that is 6 hours before the lunch. The window runs from 6 hours before to 6 hours after the lunch, so it contains the lunch, which is consistent with the lunch being the source. Food-specific attack rates are the next step.

questions.prompt: An epi curve rises steadily for three weeks and stays high. Which of the three patterns does this suggest, and what kind of source would you look for?
questions.answer: A continuous common-source outbreak: the curve “rises gradually and might plateau” (CDC, n.d.-a). Look for a source that keeps exposing people, such as a contaminated well or water supply, rather than a single meal (which would give a sharp rise and fall within one incubation period) or person-to-person spread (successive peaks one incubation period apart).

blocks.html: Spot Map and Choropleth Map

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A spot map marks each case with a dot at the place where the person lived or was exposed (CDC, 2012a). A choropleth map (area map) shades each area, such as a ward, block or district, by a rate or proportion, with darker shades for higher burden.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A spot map shows where cases are, and can reveal a cluster around a single water source or construction site. It shows only numerators. A dense cluster of dots may simply mean many people live there. The CDC’s teaching text states that a spot map “does not show risk of disease”, and that the risk “may not be particularly high if that area is densely populated” (CDC, 2012a). A choropleth map divides cases by the population of each area, so it shows risk. The CDC advises that the “intensity of shade or color reflects increasing disease burden” (CDC, 2012a).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Figure 4.12 shows 185 dengue cases in a town of nine wards (synthetic data). On the spot map, ward W5 in the centre has the most dots (54). On the choropleth map W5 is pale, and the dark wards are W9 and W3 on the eastern edge.

blocks.alt: Spot map and choropleth map of dengue by ward
blocks.caption: Figure 4.12. Spot map (left, one dot per case) and choropleth map (right, cases per 10,000 population) for the same 185 dengue cases in nine wards (synthetic teaching data).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Rate per 10,000 = cases ÷ population × 10,000.

  1. W5: 54 ÷ 45,000 × 10,000 = 12.0 per 10,000.
  2. W9: 18 ÷ 5,000 × 10,000 = 36.0 per 10,000.
  3. W3: 21 ÷ 6,000 × 10,000 = 35.0 per 10,000.
  4. Whole town: 185 ÷ 132,000 × 10,000 = 14.0 per 10,000.
  5. Result: W5 has three times as many cases as W9 (54 vs 18) but one-third of W9’s risk (12.0 vs 36.0 per 10,000). Target breeding-site control by rate (W9, W3), and plan treatment capacity by count (W5).

points.html: The spot map answers “where are the cases?”; the choropleth map answers “where is the risk highest?”. A report on an outbreak usually needs both.
A choropleth rate in a small area rests on few cases, so it is unstable: one extra case in a ward of 5,000 moves its rate by 2 per 10,000.
The choropleth map shades the whole area uniformly and hides variation within it. The picture also depends on where the boundaries are drawn.
Plot cases by residence or by place of exposure, and say which. The two can point to different places.

blocks.html: Pictogram

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A pictogram represents a quantity by a row of identical small pictures, each standing for a fixed number of units, with a fraction of a picture for a remainder.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Pictograms are built for lay audiences, such as a village health and sanitation meeting or a poster in a PHC, where a row of child figures is easier to take in than an axis. Their accuracy depends on one rule: change the number of symbols, never their size.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Figure 4.13 shows fully immunised children in four PHCs over one year (synthetic data), with one figure = 50 children. PHC A: 300 = 6 figures. PHC B: 175 = 3.5 figures. PHC C: 250 = 5 figures. PHC D: 125 = 2.5 figures.

blocks.alt: Pictogram of fully immunised children in four PHCs
blocks.caption: Figure 4.13. Pictogram: fully immunised children in four PHCs; one figure = 50 children (synthetic teaching data).

points.html: State the value of one symbol in the title or a key.
A pictogram gives only approximate values; a fraction of a symbol is hard to judge by eye. Print the numbers beside the rows when exactness matters.
Showing a larger quantity with a bigger symbol, instead of more symbols, misleads (§4.5.6).

blocks.html: Population Pyramid

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A population pyramid is a pair of back-to-back horizontal bar diagrams showing the count or percentage of a population in each age group, males on one side and females on the other (CDC, 2012b).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
The youngest age group is at the bottom and the oldest at the top. The outline records a population’s history of births and deaths. Three shapes are named (Population Education, n.d.):

  • Expansive: a broad base and a narrow top, a large share of young people. It reflects high fertility and lower life expectancy.
  • Constrictive: narrower at the bottom than in the middle, with smaller shares in the youngest age groups, after fertility has fallen.
  • Stationary: roughly equal shares across age groups, tapering only at the top, with low birth rates.

Pyramids can also show a disease or health characteristic by age and sex (CDC, 2012b).

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
The age dependency ratio summarises a pyramid in one number. It is the ratio of dependents (people aged under 15 or over 64) to the working-age population (aged 15–64), expressed per 100 working-age people (World Bank, n.d.):

dependency ratio = (population aged 0–14 + population aged 65+) ÷ population aged 15–64 × 100

It splits into a young-age ratio (0–14 ÷ 15–64 × 100) and an old-age ratio (65+ ÷ 15–64 × 100). Because the numerator and the denominator come from the same population, you can compute it from counts or from percentages.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Figure 4.14 shows two hypothetical districts (synthetic data).

blocks.alt: Population pyramids of an expansive and a constrictive population
blocks.caption: Figure 4.14. Population pyramids of two hypothetical districts, percentage of total population by age group and sex (synthetic teaching data).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Expansive district: aged 0–14, 39.44%; aged 15–64, 53.67%; aged 65+, 6.92%.
  2. Dependency ratio = (39.44 + 6.92) ÷ 53.67 × 100 = 46.36 ÷ 53.67 × 100 = 86.4 dependents per 100 working-age people. Young-age ratio 73.5; old-age ratio 12.9.
  3. Constrictive district: aged 0–14, 18.74%; aged 15–64, 69.77%; aged 65+, 11.44%.
  4. Dependency ratio = (18.74 + 11.44) ÷ 69.77 × 100 = 30.18 ÷ 69.77 × 100 = 43.3. Young-age ratio 26.9; old-age ratio 16.4.
  5. Result: the expansive district carries twice the dependency burden, almost all of it children. Its health needs are child-health and maternal services; the constrictive district’s old-age ratio is higher (16.4 vs 12.9), pointing towards non-communicable disease and geriatric care.

points.html: Plot percentages of the total population, not counts, when you compare pyramids of populations of different sizes.
Use equal age-group widths. An open-ended top group (80+) is common; do not read its bar as a five-year band.
A dent in one age group can come from a past event (a famine, an epidemic, a fall in births) or from migration: a district that sends young men away for work shows a pinched male side at ages 20–39.
The dependency ratio is a demographic ratio; it counts ages, not who actually works or depends on others.

blocks.html: Misleading Graphs

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A misleading graph gives the reader a visual impression that the numbers do not support. The deception may be deliberate or accidental; the damage to the reader is the same.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A graph encodes numbers as lengths, positions, angles or areas. It misleads when that encoding is broken. Standard texts give misleading graphs a section of their own (Bland, 2015, ch. 5). Failures to watch for:

  • Truncated baseline on a bar diagram (recall the derivation in §4.2.1).
  • Area and volume symbols: doubling a symbol’s height and width multiplies its area by 2 × 2 = 4, so a two-fold difference looks four-fold.
  • 3-D effects: tilted pies and bars with depth distort angles and lengths. The near wedge of a tilted pie looks bigger than an equal far wedge.
  • Unequal intervals on a time axis, or a histogram with unequal classes drawn by height instead of density (recall §4.3.1).
  • Two y-axes on one chart: the apparent crossing point of the lines depends entirely on how each axis was scaled.
  • An arithmetic axis for proportional change, or an unlabelled log axis (recall §4.5.1).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Two blocks report full immunisation coverage of 88% and 92% (synthetic data). Figure 4.15 draws the same two numbers twice.

blocks.alt: The same two coverage figures drawn with and without a truncated axis
blocks.caption: Figure 4.15. Full immunisation coverage in two blocks, drawn from zero (left) and from 86% (right) (synthetic teaching data).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. True ratio: 92 ÷ 88 = 1.045. Block Y’s coverage is 4.5% higher (4 percentage points).
  2. With the axis starting at 86, the drawn bars are 88 − 86 = 2 and 92 − 86 = 6 units long.
  3. Drawn ratio: 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
  4. Result: the truncated chart makes Block Y look three times as good as Block X, when it is only 1.045 times as high.

points.html: Bars and areas must start at zero. A line diagram, or a dot chart (one dot per category on a value axis), may use a narrower y-axis, because it encodes values by position, not length; mark the range clearly.
One symbol, one value: change the count of symbols, not their size.
Avoid 3-D effects on 2-D data.
Before you trust any chart, read the axis labels, the scale and the baseline before you look at the shape.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 4.5

questions.prompt: Ward P had 40 dengue cases in a population of 50,000; ward Q had 15 cases in 6,000. Which has more dots on a spot map, and which is darker on a choropleth map? Give both rates per 10,000.
questions.answer: Ward P has more dots (40 vs 15). Rates: P = 40 ÷ 50,000 × 10,000 = 8.0 per 10,000; Q = 15 ÷ 6,000 × 10,000 = 25.0 per 10,000. Ward Q is darker on the choropleth map: its risk is about three times ward P’s.

questions.prompt: A district’s population is 34% aged 0–14, 60% aged 15–64 and 6% aged 65+. Compute its age dependency ratio. Is its pyramid more likely to be expansive or constrictive?
questions.answer: Dependency ratio = (34 + 6) ÷ 60 × 100 = 66.7 dependents per 100 working-age people (young-age ratio 34 ÷ 60 × 100 = 56.7; old-age ratio 6 ÷ 60 × 100 = 10.0). A third of the population is under 15 and the burden is almost all children, so the pyramid is more likely expansive (broad base).

questions.prompt: A poster shows PHC coverage of 60% by a syringe 3 cm tall and 1 cm wide, and 90% by a syringe 4.5 cm tall and 1.5 cm wide. What ratio does the poster’s area suggest, and what is the true ratio?
questions.answer: Areas: 3 × 1 = 3 cm² and 4.5 × 1.5 = 6.75 cm². The poster suggests 6.75 ÷ 3 = 2.25 times the coverage. The true ratio is 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5. Scaling both dimensions by 1.5 multiplied the area by 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25. Draw more symbols, or bars, instead.
